# Code-along 06 {data-menu-title="Code-along" background-image="images/terminal.png"}

Download and open [code-along-06.qmd](https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/qefeakui0gn7twv9pv3nj/code-along-06.qmd?rlkey=om3xh0jc635ufmjno0axtzsrk&dl=1)

## Packages {.sparse-slide}

Load the standard packages & 1 new package: `gtsummary()`


```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: load

# Only need to install once per machine. 
# install.packages("gtsummary")

library(here)
library(tidyverse) 
library(haven) # not core tidyverse
library(gssr)
library(summarytools)
library(gtsummary) # load the new package
```

::: notes
We'll use `gtsummary()` to make pretty tables that include our
statistical tests.
:::

## Load your data {.sparse-slide}

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: gssdata

# Get the data from the 2022 survey
gss22 <- gss_get_yr(2022)

```

## Variables {.smaller}

-   `fefam` Better for man to work, woman tend home
-   `postlife` Belief in life after death\
-   `lifenow` R's rating of life overall now from 0-10
-   `premarsx` Sex before marriage
-   `agekdbrn` R's age when 1st child born
-   `sex` Respondents sex
-   `educ` Respondents highest edu credit
-   `age` Age of respondent
-   `polviews` Think of self as liberal or conservative

## Variable Management {.smaller}

::: task
{{< fa check-double >}} Make a df with only the (pretty) categorical and continuous
variables we'll analyze.
:::


```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: my-data
#| code-line-numbers: "1-6|8-15|17-18"

# Categorical Variables
my_cat <- gss22 |>
  select(id, premarsx, fefam, postlife, sex, polviews) |>
  zap_missing() |>
  as_factor() |>
  droplevels()

# Continuous Variables
my_con <- gss22 |>
  select(id, age, educ, lifenow, agekdbrn) |>
  mutate(
    age = as.numeric(age),
    educ = as.numeric(educ),
    lifenow = as.numeric(lifenow),
    agekdbrn = as.numeric(agekdbrn))

# Combine the two dataframes
my_data <- left_join(my_cat, my_con, by = "id")
```

# $chi^2$ Test {.theme-section}

## [$chi^2$]{style="color: #18BC9C"} test {.sparse-slide}

[$chi^2$]{style="color: #18BC9C"} determines if categorical variables
are related

<br>

Tests if the rows and columns in a two-way table are independent

## [$chi^2$]{style="color: #18BC9C"} in action

The news has been reporting a large gender difference in attitudes about
gender roles.

You evaluate this narrative using the variable `fefam`:

> It is much better for everyone involved if the man is the achiever
> outside the home and the woman takes care of the home and family.

<br>

. . .

::: task
{{< fa lightbulb >}} How do you test your hypothesis?
:::

##  {.quiz-question data-menu-title="Knowledge Check" background-image="images/clipboard-question.png" background-size="100px" background-repeat="repeat"}

::: {style="color: #F39C12"}
{{< fa clipboard-question >}} Which of these equations represents your
**research** hypothesis?
:::

-   [There is no association between gender identity and attitudes about
    gender roles (statistically
    independent).]{data-explanation="😲 But you think there is a relationship."}
-   [Gender identity and attitudes about gender roles are related in the
    population (statistically
    independent).]{data-explanation="😲 They are INdependent?"}
-   [Gender identity and attitudes about gender roles are related in the
    population (statistically dependent).]{.correct
    data-explanation="💯 Correct!"}

##  {.quiz-question data-menu-title="Knowledge Check" background-image="images/clipboard-question.png" background-size="100px" background-repeat="repeat"}

::: {style="color: #F39C12"}
{{< fa clipboard-question >}} Which of these equations represents your
**null** hypothesis?
:::

-   [There is no association between gender identity and attitudes about
    gender roles (statistically independent).]{.correct
    data-explanation="💯 Correct!"}
-   [Gender identity and attitudes about gender roles are related in the
    population (statistically
    independent).]{data-explanation="😲 The null hypothesis is always no relationship."}
-   [There is no association between gender identity and attitudes about
    gender roles (statistically
    dependent).]{data-explanation="😲 They are dependent?"}

## Review: Pretty cross-tab

Use `summarytools::ctable`

```{r}
#| label: ctable
#| output-location: fragment

ctable(my_data$fefam, my_data$sex, # <1>
  prop = "c", # <2>
  format = "p", # <3>
  useNA = "no"
) # <4>
```

1.  Change from `table()` to `ctable()`.
2.  The "c" gives column %; "r" would give row %.
3.  This adds the % symbols to the table.
4.  Exclude the missing levels from the table.

## Pretty cross-tab (new)

Now that we know how to use the `dplyr |>`!

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-cross
#| code-line-numbers: "1-2|3-4|5-6"
#| output-location: fragment

my_data |>
  tbl_cross(
    row = fefam,
    col = sex,
    percent = "column",
    missing = "no")
```

## Pretty cross-tab with `p-value`

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-cross-p
#| code-line-numbers: "1-6|7"
#| output-location: fragment

my_data |>
  tbl_cross(
    row = fefam,
    col = sex,
    percent = "column",
    missing = "no") |>
  add_p(source_note = TRUE)
```

##  {.quiz-question data-menu-title="Knowledge Check" background-image="images/clipboard-question.png" background-size="100px" background-repeat="repeat"}

::: {style="color: #F39C12"}
{{< fa clipboard-question >}} Which of these statements best summarizes
your conclusion?
:::

-   [Our findings prove that gender identity has no effect on attitudes
    about gender roles]{data-explanation="😲 We can't PROVE anything."}
-   [Since the p-value is above 0.05, we can conclude that gender
    identity strongly influences attitudes about gender
    roles.]{data-explanation="😲 A high p-value indicates weak evidence against the null hypothesis"}
-   [We find no statistically significant relationship between gender
    identity and attitudes about gender roles.]{.correct
    data-explanation="💯 Correct!"}

## Caution: size matters

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: sample-size
#| code-line-numbers: "1-2"
#| output-location: fragment

my_data |>
  filter(age < 21) |>
  tbl_cross(
    row = fefam,
    col = sex,
    percent = "column",
    missing = "no") |>
  add_p(source_note = TRUE)
```

::: notes
Our sample size is relatively small once we filtered out people older
than 25. We have 88 people between the ages of 18-20 in our new sample,
which is greater than the 50 observations necessary to assume the
sampling distribution of the means is normal.

Yet, the frequency in each individual cell is quite small. Typically,
each cell should have no fewer than 30 people to make meaningful
statistical calculations.

In other words, large standard errors should be interpreted as an
imprecise estimate, not as an indication that the null hypothesis is
valid.
:::

## Review: `t.test()` with proportions

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: t.test

# Use logic to recode factor as mean (yes = 1; no: 2 = 0)
my_data$ghosts <- ifelse(my_data$postlife == "yes", 1, 0)

# t.test
t.test(my_data$ghosts ~ my_data$sex, alternative = "two.sided")

```

## `t.test()` & [$chi^2$]{style="color: #18BC9C"}

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: postlife

my_data |>
  tbl_cross(
    row = ghosts,
    col = sex,
    percent = "column",
    missing = "no") |>
  add_p(source_note = TRUE)

```

# Pearson’s Correlation Coefficient (R) {.theme-section}

## `cor.test()` {.sparse-slide}

R is the correlation between two interval-ratio variables.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| eval: false
#| label: cor.test

cor.test(
  ~ v1 + v2,
  data = your_dataframe,
  method = "pearson",
  na.action = na.omit
  ) 
```

<br>

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## {{< fa hat-wizard >}} Heads Up!

Because Pearson's R doesn't require specifying an independent and
dependent variable, the order of the variables does not matter.
:::

## Scatterplot

```{r}
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| label: scatterplot-educ

my_data %>%
  drop_na(educ, agekdbrn) |>
  filter(agekdbrn < 50) |>
ggplot(aes(x = educ, y = agekdbrn)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.5, color = "#18BC9C") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs( title    = "Years of education\nby age when 1st child born",
        caption  = "US General Social Survey (2022)")
```

## `cor.test()` in action

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: cor-educ01
#| output-location: fragment

cor.test(
  ~ educ + agekdbrn,
  data = my_data,
  method = "pearson",
  na.action = na.omit
)

```

## Tidy `cor.test()`

::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: cor-educ02

# Save results
my_test <- cor.test(
  ~ educ + agekdbrn,
  data = my_data,
  method = "pearson",
  na.action = na.omit
)
```
:::

::: {.column .fragment width="55%"}
```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: cor-educ03

# Create a tibble with key stats
cor_summary <- tibble(
  correlation = my_test$estimate,
  p_value     = my_test$p.value,
  conf_low    = my_test$conf.int[1],
  conf_high   = my_test$conf.int[2]
)
```
:::
:::::

<br>

. . .

```{r}
#| message: false
#| label: cor-educ04

cor_summary
```

## `cor.test()` & `t.test()` {.smaller}

:::: panel-tabset
### Equivalence

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## {{< fa hat-wizard >}} Heads Up!

Correlating a dichotomous variable and a continuous variable is
equivalent to doing a t-test on that continuous variable by the
dichotomous variable.
:::

<br>

When x is coded as 0/1, these formulas yield equivalent p-values, even
if the t-statistics look slightly different due to rounding or variance
assumptions.

### `cor.test()`

```{r}
#| label: sex01

# Create numeric version of sex
my_data <- my_data %>%
  mutate(female = if_else(sex == "female", 1, 0))

cor.test(
  ~ female + lifenow,
  data = my_data,
  method = "pearson",
  na.action = na.omit
)
```

### `t.test()`

```{r}
#| label: sex02

t.test(my_data$lifenow ~ my_data$sex, alternative = "two.sided")

```
::::

# {data-menu-title="Summary" .smaller}

| Feature | t-test | Chi-square test | Pearson’s Correlation (R) |
|------------------|------------------|-------------------|------------------|
| Purpose | Compare means between groups | Test association between categories | Measure linear relationship strength |
| Data Type | Continuous (numeric) | Categorical (nominal or ordinal) | Continuous (numeric) |
| Variables Required | 1 dependent, 1 independent | 2 categorical variables | 2 continuous variables |
| Directionality | One-tailed or two-tailed | Non-directional | Indicates direction (+/-) and strength |
| Example Question | Do men and women differ in time spent on housework ? | Is marital status associated with political party identity? | Is there a correlation between number of children and parental stress? |
